description: An inspiration for undergraduates to take courage and deal with real life problems concerning space challenges. A group for personal and grupal development inspired by the idea of making a little footstep on Human history.
summary:
Picking a landing spot on the Moon is tricky: the terrain is rough, the Sun can vanish for days, and Earth isn’t always in sight. So we built an interactive 2D and 3D lunar map that puts all of that in one place.
Choose any point on the Moon, or jump to a past mission like Apollo, and the app shows you the real horizon, where the Sun and Earth are in the sky, and a live countdown to sunset or Earthset. It uses NASA’s LOLA terrain data and SPICE ephemerides, so the numbers are solid. Each site gets rated as optimal, normal, or not recommended based on slope, roughness, sunlight, temperature, and radiation. You can even compare sites side by side and test solar panel setups, which is key near the poles.
Why does it matter? Missions get one shot at landing, and plans change fast. Our tool helps teams react quickly, choose safer sites, and see exactly which assumptions are behind every result. It’s also a fun way for anyone to explore the Moon!
details:
We developed an interactive lunar map that brings together the information needed to design a mission, as well as to learn about the Moon for educational purposes.

LunarBee displays the Moon in 2D or 3D for better visualization. You can choose which map layer to look at: topography, radiation dose, sky-view factor, or resource indices. A catalog of past and planned missions is shown as markers on the surface for reference, and you can compare those sites against each other and against new points of your choice.

For any selected point, LunarBee estimates how the Sun and Earth appear from there and uses those results to compare candidate landing sites. For each site, the program computes the azimuth and elevation of both bodies from SPICE ephemerides (DE440, with light-time and stellar aberration corrections), measures the observer’s position on the lunar surface to account for parallax, and derives the time remaining until the next sunset, sunrise, or Earthset.

For sites south of 60°S, we also build a horizon profile from NASA LOLA polar elevation models (10 to 240 m per pixel). Rays are traced across 360° of azimuth out to 200 km, including lunar curvature. The Sun and Earth are treated as discs with angular radii of about 0.27° and 0.95°, so the visible fraction is integrated over the horizon rather than reduced to a visible/not visible flag. This matters near the poles, where the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon. From these series we obtain illumination percentage, longest continuous night, and Earth visibility. Slope, roughness, and safe area are computed from the fine DEM, and each criterion is classified as optimal, normal, or not recommended. This rating shows how different locations have very different conditions, which makes the app a clear, visual way to learn.

It also displays the data for each chosen location, such as ephemeris data, the positions of the Sun and Earth, and the angle of radiation incidence. You can enter your own coordinates and the mission duration, then watch the simulation update the parameters and the graphics.

It is written in Python, using NumPy and SciPy for the numerical work, SpiceyPy for ephemerides, Rasterio and PyProj for the DEMs, and PySide6 for the interface. JPL Horizons is used only to cross-check the SPICE results. It runs on a standard computer.

Several design decisions shaped the result. We made every tab use the same ephemeris calculation, so a given instant returns identical values everywhere. Users can also choose the quality of the maps, with recommended downloads suggested, and delete them when they are done. Our goal is to support early-stage site screening and to give students a quantitative way to see why the lunar poles are so interesting.
